query: How mask mandates help Covid-19 cases, and what did the study find?
draft_answer: Mask mandates appear to help reduce COVID-19 cases by lowering transmission when they are adopted and followed consistently, and several studies in the summaries support this effect at different levels of evidence [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9729715||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC9190185||ABSTRACT||000]. In US state-level data, the study found that mask mandates could offset about one third of the increase in case growth associated with a rise in mobility, and a hypothetical national mandate on May 15, 2020 was estimated to reduce total infections by 23.7% to 30.4% by November 15, 2020 [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000]. Another study found that mask mandates in place for at least two months were associated with lower monthly incidence than having no prevention measure or having one in place for less than a month, with larger reductions seen in high-social-vulnerability counties [pmc_PMC9729715||ABSTRACT||001]. The healthcare-worker reviews also found that face masks significantly protected against infection, with especially strong support for N95 masks, while surgical masks were reported to protect better than cloth masks [pmc_PMC9190185||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9845060||ABSTRACT||001]. One modeling paper adds that masks work best when combined with upward ventilation, whereas masks used inappropriately with ventilation could be counterproductive [pmc_PMC9803700||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the studies agree that masks are beneficial, but they also suggest that effectiveness depends on compliance, duration, mask type, and the surrounding environment [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9729715||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC9803700||ABSTRACT||001].

limitations_and_uncertainty: Several findings come from observational or modeled evidence, so they estimate associations or projected effects rather than proving direct causation [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9803700||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How sustainability reporting link with SDGs and sustainability performance, it matter from the supply chain framework too?
draft_answer:
Across the papers, sustainability reporting is generally portrayed as a way to connect corporate actions to the SDGs, but the strength of that connection varies by context and methodology. One line of evidence argues that sustainability reporting can support SDG implementation by measuring environmental performance and using materiality matrices to incorporate stakeholder views, thereby improving report quality [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||001]. Another study similarly presents corporate sustainability reporting, especially under GRI guidelines, as a tool to assess whether SDGs matter to the private sector and how companies contribute to them [https://openalex.org/W4220859323||ABSTRACT||000]. However, this positive framing is complicated by evidence from a large cross-company study showing no correlation in reporting specific SDGs and a disconnect between SDG reporting and actual corporate sustainability performance, suggesting firms may report SDGs arbitrarily rather than based on performance [https://openalex.org/W4394576889||ABSTRACT||000].

From a supply chain perspective, several papers indicate that the reporting-to-SDG link becomes more meaningful when sustainability is assessed across suppliers, value-chain actors, and product life cycles. One study finds that sustainable supply chain management is positively and significantly related to financial performance, SDGs, and the relationship between sustainable supply chains and SDGs, and it explicitly recommends implementing sustainability from supplier to customer to improve operational efficiency and reduce environmental and social impacts [https://openalex.org/W4394886303||ABSTRACT||001]. A separate supply-chain framework paper proposes 91 environmental and social indicators so companies can measure both their own and their suppliers’ sustainability performance while improving transparency and accountability [https://openalex.org/W4400657024||ABSTRACT||000]. Likewise, another paper argues that SDGs and life-cycle sustainability assessment are complementary, and that linking LCSA to SDGs can improve transparency and consistency in reporting sustainability performance of product systems [https://openalex.org/W4281493513||ABSTRACT||001].

At the same time, the literature repeatedly notes gaps in current SDG reporting practices. In tourism, companies may cite SDGs in reports but still fail to explain how sustainability initiatives shape their contribution to the goals [https://openalex.org/W4220859323||ABSTRACT||000]. A Sri Lankan corporate reporting study found SDG 12 and SDG 15 were most frequently reported and introduced a score index integrating SDGs, but it did not provide supply-chain-specific evidence [https://openalex.org/W4392003298||ABSTRACT||001]. More broadly, one paper says SDGs and LCSA are complementary but there is no harmonized way to link them yet, while another says GRI-based supply-chain indicators are useful for SDG-oriented measurement but does not explicitly treat sustainability reporting as a separate construct [https://openalex.org/W4380365728||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4327714039||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence suggests sustainability reporting matters most when it is tied to concrete performance indicators and supply-chain or life-cycle analysis, but current reporting often remains incomplete, inconsistent, or weakly connected to actual sustainability outcomes [https://openalex.org/W4394576889||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400657024||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: Sustainability reporting is presented as a tool for linking corporate activity to the SDGs by measuring environmental performance and incorporating stakeholder views, but evidence also shows that firms may report SDGs without a clear connection to actual sustainability performance [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4394576889||ABSTRACT||000].

Supply-chain-oriented studies suggest that sustainability reporting becomes more actionable when it measures performance across suppliers, value-chain actors, or product life cycles, improving transparency and accountability [https://openalex.org/W4400657024||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4281493513||ABSTRACT||001].

A study of sustainable supply chains reports positive and significant relationships with both financial performance and SDGs, and explicitly recommends sustainability implementation from supplier to customer [https://openalex.org/W4394886303||ABSTRACT||001].

Some reporting studies show that companies mention SDGs but do not explain how sustainability initiatives contribute to them, indicating a gap between disclosure and substantive performance [https://openalex.org/W4220859323||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4392003298||ABSTRACT||001].

The literature does not yet offer a harmonized way to connect SDGs with life-cycle sustainability assessment, and further research is needed to consistently link metrics to goals [https://openalex.org/W4380365728||ABSTRACT||001].

limitations_and_uncertainty: Several summaries explicitly note missing supply-chain evidence, so not every paper can support conclusions about supply-chain-based sustainability reporting [https://openalex.org/W4394576889||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4220859323||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4392003298||ABSTRACT||001].

The evidence is mixed: some studies report positive links between SDGs, sustainability reporting, and performance, while others find SDG reporting disconnected from actual sustainability performance [https://openalex.org/W4394886303||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4394576889||ABSTRACT||000].

There is no general consensus or harmonized framework for connecting SDGs with life-cycle or supply-chain assessment, so the field still needs clearer indicators and methods [https://openalex.org/W4380365728||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4327714039||ABSTRACT||000].

query: In the sustainability assessment of district heating systems, which multi-criteria decision analysis methods were compared, and what did the sensitivity analysis reveal about their suitability and differences in calculation and interpretation?
draft_answer: The district-heating sustainability assessment paper compared five multi-criteria decision analysis methods: WSM, TOPSIS, PROMETHEE, ELECTRE, and DEA, using eight criteria for 12 district heating companies [W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. Its sensitivity analysis varied criterion weights in three ways: changing weights individually to examine stability ranges for alternatives, changing them individually by a fixed amount to observe effects on average scores, and comparing AHP-based weighting with equal weighting [W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. The authors concluded that all five methods are suitable for sustainability analyses of district heating systems, but they differ in calculation process and in how results are interpreted [W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. This aligns with broader sustainability-method literature showing that MCDA/MCDM frameworks are commonly used and that AHP is frequently used in sustainability-oriented evaluation, although those sources do not specify the same district-heating comparison [W4315708900||ABSTRACT||001]. Related reviews also emphasize that methodological choice affects how alternatives, criteria, indicators, weights, uncertainty, and interpretation are handled, and call for greater transparency in why particular methods are chosen [W3204246278||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence suggests that the district-heating study’s main contribution was not that one method was universally superior, but that multiple methods can be acceptable while producing different computational pathways and interpretive outputs [W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How are the SDOs linked to policy coherance for sustainable development in the EU context?
draft_answer: Across the papers, the SDGs are linked to policy coherence for sustainable development in the EU as both a normative framework and an analytical tool for aligning policies across sectors and levels of governance [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||000]. Several studies treat coherence as the degree to which EU strategies such as the European Green Deal, the 2030 Agenda, the Circular Economy strategy, and the European Semester Country-Specific Recommendations are co-integrated, with mapping or correlation exercises used to assess alignment [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W3209532954||ABSTRACT||000]. In this view, the SDGs help identify whether progress in one area undermines another, and they also provide a basis for monitoring where coherence is weakest, especially in environmental goals [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000]. The literature also suggests that coherence depends on how implementation tools are designed: Life Cycle Assessment is presented as a way to support policy design and monitoring for SDG and Green Deal ambitions, while the Planetary Boundaries framework adds an absolute sustainability dimension [https://openalex.org/W4210270578||ABSTRACT||000]. However, the papers also emphasize that policy coherence is not purely technical; it is shaped by political ideas, institutions, and interests, and depoliticized or “neutral” SDG arrangements may limit transformative change [https://openalex.org/W4308113945||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000]. Empirically, the EU appears to have incorporated the SDGs into its strategic priorities, but gaps remain because some major challenges are not reflected in the CSRs and environmental goals remain the least coherent [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||001][https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000]. More broadly, the evidence points to a need for a system perspective, better trade-off analysis, and context-specific priorities to strengthen policy coherence across governance levels and scales [https://openalex.org/W4366975340||ABSTRACT||001].

key_claims.claim: The SDGs are used in the EU literature as a framework for assessing and improving policy coherence across major strategies such as the European Green Deal, the 2030 Agenda, the Circular Economy strategy, and the European Semester CSRs [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W3209532954||ABSTRACT||000].

Policy coherence for sustainable development is presented as both a technical alignment problem and a political one, because coherence depends on ideas, institutions, and interests as well as on governance arrangements [https://openalex.org/W4308113945||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000].

Quantitative and mapping studies suggest that the EU has incorporated the SDGs into its strategic priorities, but important gaps remain, including some major challenges not captured by the CSRs and environmental goals that are especially incoherent [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||001][https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000].

Life Cycle Assessment and the Planetary Boundaries framework are proposed as tools that can strengthen EU policy design and monitoring for SDG achievement while accounting for absolute sustainability limits [https://openalex.org/W4210270578||ABSTRACT||000].

The literature recommends a system perspective, trade-off analysis, and context-specific priorities to improve policy coherence across governance levels and implementation scales [https://openalex.org/W4366975340||ABSTRACT||001].

limitations_and_uncertainty: Several papers are conceptual or framework-oriented, so the evidence on causal effects of the SDGs on policy coherence is limited to proposed alignments and correlations rather than direct policy impact [https://openalex.org/W3209532954||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4210270578||ABSTRACT||000].

The evidence base is uneven across policy areas and countries: some findings focus on the Netherlands, SDG 9, SDG 11, or selected EU instruments, which limits how far the results can be generalized to the whole EU [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4312225363||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4362550191||ABSTRACT||000].

One paper notes poor intra-cluster connections in the research literature itself, suggesting that more transdisciplinary work is needed before the SDGs-policy coherence relationship in the EU can be fully synthesized [https://openalex.org/W4366975340||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How do the themes of "Environmental sustainability", "Sustainability implementation barriers", and "Sustainable residential buildings" connect when comparing off-site construction research with the barrier analysis in Ghana and the "Mostadam" approach in Saudi Arabia, and what sustainability-related findings are highlighted across these contexts?
draft_answer: Across the supplied studies, the connecting thread is that sustainability in the built environment is treated both as a design/performance goal and as an implementation challenge. The Southern Africa off-site construction study shows that prefabricated construction methods can mainstream sustainability into affordable housing, with better overall sustainability performance for innovative prefabricated construction methods under sustainability-related metrics, including lifecycle energy and cost considerations [https://openalex.org/W4386401188||ABSTRACT||000]. In Ghana, sustainability is framed through environmental performance and residential-building implementation: one study found that environmental indicators across the full building life cycle were all important, especially water quality, air quality, energy use and conservation, and environmental compliance and management [https://openalex.org/W3168941981||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W3168941981||ABSTRACT||001]. A second Ghana study on residential buildings shows that sustainability must be integrated throughout development but is hindered by management, standards, society, and knowledge barriers, with management-related barriers identified as the most significant obstacle to implementation [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||001]. This aligns with the Ghana retrofit barrier analysis, which also emphasizes cultural, economic, technical knowledge, and regulatory barriers as obstacles to sustainability in the built environment [https://openalex.org/W4293340752||ABSTRACT||001]. More generally, the barrier-focused papers agree that sustainability progress depends on addressing education, incentives, lifecycle-cost awareness, and policy support rather than relying on technical solutions alone [https://openalex.org/W3145060410||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W3132259306||ABSTRACT||000]. In Saudi Arabia, the Mostadam discussion places sustainable residential buildings within a broader Vision 2030 transition toward sustainable buildings and cities, presenting the framework as a pathway to comprehensive sustainable development at both building and city scales [https://openalex.org/W3120903819||ABSTRACT||001]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that environmental sustainability, sustainable residential buildings, and implementation barriers are interdependent: technical approaches such as off-site construction and rating frameworks like Mostadam define what sustainable buildings can look like, while Ghana- and Iran-based barrier analyses explain why achieving them is difficult in practice [https://openalex.org/W4386401188||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W3120903819||ABSTRACT||001][https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||001][https://openalex.org/W3132259306||ABSTRACT||000].

Another summary describes DECISION as a multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled phase III study in locally advanced/metastatic RAI-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer, designed to assess whether sorafenib improves progression-free survival [pmc_PMC3164634||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC3164634||ABSTRACT||001]. The treatment schedule differed by source: one record summary reports HRQoL assessments at baseline, every 8 weeks until Week 24, then every 16 weeks and at the off-treatment visit, using EQ-5D-3L and FACT-G with completion/compliance, mean change from baseline, and time to first and definitive deterioration as outcomes [pmc_PMC9972135||ABSTRACT||000], while the other reports treatment continuing until progression, unacceptable toxicity, noncompliance, or withdrawal of consent, with efficacy every 56 days and safety every 28 days for the first 8 months then every 56 days thereafter [pmc_PMC3164634||ABSTRACT||001]. The primary endpoint reported for the sorafenib DECISION study is progression-free survival, with secondary endpoints including overall survival, time to disease progression, disease control rate, response rate, duration of response, safety, and pharmacokinetic analysis [pmc_PMC3164634||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC3164634||ABSTRACT||002]. The trial registration identifiers also differ across the summaries: one gives ClinicalTrials.gov Number NCT02702388 [pmc_PMC9972135||ABSTRACT||002], while the other gives NCT00984282 [pmc_PMC3164634||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC3164634||ABSTRACT||002]. Several other summaries explicitly state that they do not provide ClinicalTrials.gov record details, so the evidence base is limited to these two partially overlapping descriptions [pmc_PMC5384304||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC5386727||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC5386727||ABSTRACT||001].

key_claims.claim: One summary describes DECISION as a phase 3 randomized, double-blind study in radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer with lenvatinib starting doses of 18 mg/day or 24 mg/day [pmc_PMC9972135||ABSTRACT||000].

Another summary describes DECISION as a multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled phase III study in locally advanced/metastatic RAI-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer designed to test whether sorafenib improves progression-free survival [pmc_PMC3164634||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC3164634||ABSTRACT||001].

The treatment schedule reported in one summary includes HRQoL assessments at baseline, every 8 weeks until Week 24, then every 16 weeks and at the off-treatment visit, using EQ-5D-3L and FACT-G [pmc_PMC9972135||ABSTRACT||000].

The other summary reports treatment continuing until progression, unacceptable toxicity, noncompliance, or withdrawal of consent, with efficacy every 56 days and safety every 28 days for the first 8 months then every 56 days thereafter [pmc_PMC3164634||ABSTRACT||001].

The primary endpoint reported for the sorafenib DECISION study is progression-free survival, and the secondary endpoints include overall survival, time to disease progression, disease control rate, response rate, duration of response, safety, and pharmacokinetic analysis [pmc_PMC3164634||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC3164634||ABSTRACT||002].

The trial registration identifiers given in the summaries are NCT02702388 and NCT00984282, indicating inconsistent identifiers across the provided evidence [pmc_PMC9972135||ABSTRACT||002] [pmc_PMC3164634||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC3164634||ABSTRACT||002].

query: How did broiler chicks in Iraq compare in maternal derived antibodies against Newcastle disease vaccination, and which strain performed better in the study?
draft_answer: In the Iraqi study of 1-day-old imported broiler chicks from Mosul governorate, maternal derived antibodies against Newcastle disease vaccination were assessed in Cobb 500 and Ross 308 flocks using 707 blood samples [pmc_PMC9805781||ABSTRACT||000]. Both strains showed high and fairly uniform maternal antibody titers, but Cobb 500 performed better overall than Ross 308 [pmc_PMC9805781||ABSTRACT||001]. Specifically, Cobb 500 had a higher antibody-positive rate (100% vs 97.78%), a higher mean maternal antibody titer (9,871.47 vs 8,647.76), a lower mean CV (12.41% vs 15.18%), and a higher mean vaccination index (966.59 vs 821.60) [pmc_PMC9805781||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC9805781||ABSTRACT||001]. The authors concluded that both strains had high and uniform titers, but Cobb 500 produced chicks with higher protective titers than Ross 308 [pmc_PMC9805781||ABSTRACT||001]. No other provided paper offered relevant Newcastle disease data for broiler chicks in Iraq, so the strain comparison rests on this single study [pmc_PMC10141882||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC9967544||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC10059746||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC4172590||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: In an Iraqi study of imported 1-day-old broiler chicks from Mosul governorate, maternal derived antibodies against Newcastle disease vaccination were compared between Cobb 500 and Ross 308 flocks [pmc_PMC9805781||ABSTRACT||000].

Cobb 500 chicks performed better than Ross 308 chicks, with 100% antibody positivity versus 97.78%, a higher mean maternal antibody titer, a lower mean CV, and a higher mean vaccination index [pmc_PMC9805781||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC9805781||ABSTRACT||001].
The study concluded that both strains had high and uniform maternal antibody titers, but Cobb 500 produced chicks with higher protective titers than Ross 308 [pmc_PMC9805781||ABSTRACT||001].

The other provided summaries were unrelated to Newcastle disease in Iraqi broiler chicks and therefore did not contribute additional evidence for the strain comparison [pmc_PMC10141882||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC9967544||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC10059746||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC4172590||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The evidence for this question comes from a single Iraqi study, so the comparison is not independently replicated in the supplied summaries [pmc_PMC9805781||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC9805781||ABSTRACT||001].
The summary does not provide details on study design beyond the sampled flocks and blood samples, so broader generalization to all broiler chicks in Iraq is uncertain [pmc_PMC9805781||ABSTRACT||000].

No additional Newcastle disease studies in the provided set address broiler chicks in Iraq, limiting cross-study confirmation of the Cobb 500 versus Ross 308 difference [pmc_PMC10141882||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC9967544||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC10059746||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC4172590||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How mask mandates help Covid-19 cases, and what did the study find?
draft_answer: Across the studies, mask mandates and mask use were generally associated with fewer COVID-19 cases or reduced transmission, especially when compliance and other controls were strong [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9729715||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9482873||ABSTRACT||001]. A U.S. state-level analysis found that mask mandates were more effective in states with higher compliance, and estimated that a national mask mandate starting May 15, 2020 could have lowered total U.S. infections by 23.7% to 30.4% by November 15, 2020 [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000]. The same study also found that mask mandates could offset about one third of the case-growth increase associated with a one-standard-deviation rise in mobility, suggesting mandates helped blunt transmission when people were moving around more [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000]. A separate county-level study found that behavioral policies, including face mask mandates, were linked to lower COVID-19 incidence when they were in place for at least 2 months, compared with less than 1 month or no policy [pmc_PMC9729715||ABSTRACT||000]. Other papers support the same direction of effect by reporting that face masks significantly protected healthcare workers from infection, with evidence especially supporting N95 masks, and that surgical masks outperformed cloth masks in healthcare settings [pmc_PMC9190185||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9845060||ABSTRACT||001]. Several summaries also emphasize that masks work best when combined with other measures such as social distancing, hand cleanliness, cohorting, and proper ventilation, and that poor pairing with ventilation can reduce effectiveness [pmc_PMC9482873||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4221110503||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9803700||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the study findings point to masks helping reduce cases, but the effect depends on adherence, type of mask, and whether masks are combined with other interventions [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9845060||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC9803700||ABSTRACT||001].

key_claims.claim: A U.S. state-level study found mask mandates were more effective in states with higher compliance and estimated a national mask mandate could have reduced total U.S. infections by 23.7% to 30.4% by November 15, 2020 [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000]
A county-level study found that behavioral policies including face mask mandates were associated with lower COVID-19 incidence when in place for at least 2 months [pmc_PMC9729715||ABSTRACT||000]

Mask use significantly protected healthcare workers from infection, with evidence especially supporting N95 masks, and surgical masks provided better protection than cloth masks in one review [pmc_PMC9190185||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9845060||ABSTRACT||001]

Masks were described as most effective when combined with other measures such as social distancing, hand cleanliness, cohorting, and proper ventilation [pmc_PMC9482873||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4221110503||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9803700||ABSTRACT||001]

limitations_and_uncertainty: The evidence comes from different study designs and settings, including healthcare workers, U.S. states and counties, and a youth camp outbreak, so the magnitude of benefit may not be directly comparable across contexts [pmc_PMC9190185||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9482873||ABSTRACT||001].

Some findings depend on compliance, mask type, and co-interventions such as ventilation or distancing, so mask mandates alone may not produce the same effect in all settings [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9803700||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC9482873||ABSTRACT||001].

At least one review reported no effect for gloves and gowns and noted that some protective effects were not statistically significant, indicating that not all PPE-related interventions had clear evidence [pmc_PMC9190185||ABSTRACT||001].

One summary explicitly states that evidence was insufficient to say exactly how mask mandates helped COVID-19 cases in the context of containment strategies, because it discussed non-pharmaceutical interventions more generally rather than mask mandates specifically [https://openalex.org/W3215618709||ABSTRACT||000].

query: Why nano-enhancers better for workpiece burn?
draft_answer: Across the machining-focused papers, nano-enhancers are described as better for workpiece burn mainly because they improve heat dissipation, lubrication, and anti-friction behavior during cutting or grinding [pmc_PMC9971250||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4206313494||ABSTRACT||000]. One paper specifically says carbon nanotubes raise thermal conductivity in conventional fluids, which improves heat removal and is linked to better load-carrying capacity and wear resistance, helping explain performance gains in burn-related conditions [pmc_PMC9971250||ABSTRACT||001]. Another review says nano-enhanced biolubricants outperform biolubricant-based MQL because of advanced lubrication and heat-transfer mechanisms, including distinctive film formation, atomization, and infiltration behavior [https://openalex.org/W4206313494||ABSTRACT||000]. For titanium alloy machining, the literature recommends nano-enhancers because their high thermal conductivity helps solve the “burn puzzle,” and it also notes that high hardness and spherical shape are desirable properties [https://openalex.org/W4313508734||ABSTRACT||001]. The same source suggests nano-enhancers can be part of a strategy for nickel-based alloy surface burn, alongside high-viscosity biolubricants with high fatty acid saturation, which shows that nano-enhancers are often presented as one component of a broader solution rather than a stand-alone fix [https://openalex.org/W4313508734||ABSTRACT||001]. A separate review adds that nanofluids are considered promising because of their excellent thermophysical properties, but they are still developmental and need more study to become cost-effective [https://openalex.org/W4294292954||ABSTRACT||001]. That review also notes that alternative methods are not yet mature enough and may underperform in tribological properties, surface finish, cutting forces, and working-fluid consumption, which supports the comparative advantage of nano-enhancers in machining performance [https://openalex.org/W4294292954||ABSTRACT||001]. query: What role did hexagonal boron nitride play in the study of canola oil as a bio-lubricant, and what details are provided about its evaluation?
draft_answer: Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) played the role of a solid lubricant nano-additive in a canola oil bio-lubricant study, where it was added to canola oil specifically to improve tribological performance because canola oil alone was described as underperforming relative to petroleum-based oils [https://openalex.org/W4200600140||ABSTRACT||000]. The study tested canola oil with hBN loadings of 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5 wt.% and evaluated the formulations by measuring dynamic viscosity, coefficient of friction (COF), and wear in the boundary lubrication regime using pin-on-disk tests [https://openalex.org/W4200600140||ABSTRACT||000]. Among those formulations, 1.0 wt.% hBN gave the lowest COF, reported as 40% lower than the base oil [https://openalex.org/W4200600140||ABSTRACT||000]. The same paper also reports canola-oil mixtures combining graphene nanoplatelets (GNP) and hBN in different ratios, with the combined additives showing better performance than either additive alone and an optimum synergy that reduced friction by 56% and wear by 90% versus base oil [https://openalex.org/W4200600140||ABSTRACT||001]. In contrast, several other supplied papers only mention hBN in broad reviews of sustainable or nano-enhanced biolubricants and do not provide canola-oil-specific experimental results or evaluation details [https://openalex.org/W4327639096||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4386898801||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4390658388||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4206313494||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence indicates that hBN was investigated as an additive to enhance canola oil’s lubrication behavior, with performance assessed through viscosity, friction, and wear measurements under boundary-lubrication pin-on-disk testing [https://openalex.org/W4200600140||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How FT's do they add their own personal interpretation to sustainability requirements when they fulfill their boundary-spanning role?
draft_answer: The evidence suggests that FT-like boundary-spanning actors often do not simply transmit sustainability requirements unchanged; rather, they frequently interpret and adapt them through their own role, perceptions, and local context [https://openalex.org/W4223934530||ABSTRACT||000]. In one study, directors and middle managers applied sustainability differently depending on organizational role and personal perceptions, producing different meanings across levels and functions and implying that boundary-spanning work includes sensemaking as well as translation [https://openalex.org/W4223934530||ABSTRACT||000]. A related finding shows that middle managers treated sustainability requirements through a department-specific lens and prioritized or adapted practices differently across functions, again indicating practical interpretation during implementation [https://openalex.org/W4396791633||ABSTRACT||000]. Another paper argues that organizational sustainability identity is socially constructed through employees’ convictions about core operations and customer collaboration, not mainly through formal controls, which suggests that personal beliefs can shape how sustainability requirements are framed in practice [https://openalex.org/W4285585775||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the literature also emphasizes that sustainability implementation is strengthened by shared ownership, informal communication, and collaborative planning, which can reduce purely individual discretion and align interpretations across stakeholders [https://openalex.org/W3173999974||ABSTRACT||001]. More broadly, sustainability is shown to be interpreted in multiple ways in project management research, reinforcing the idea that there is no single uniform meaning of sustainability requirements [https://openalex.org/W3189889143||ABSTRACT||000]. However, several papers explicitly note that they do not directly study FTs or boundary-spanning roles, so the evidence for FT-specific personal interpretation remains indirect rather than definitive [https://openalex.org/W4309402460||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4410729659||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3173999974||ABSTRACT||001].

query: In the sustainability assessment of district heating systems, which multi-criteria decision analysis methods were compared, and what did the sensitivity analysis reveal about their suitability and differences in calculation and interpretation?
draft_answer: For the sustainability assessment of district heating systems, one study explicitly compared five MCDA methods: WSM, TOPSIS, PROMETHEE, ELECTRE, and DEA, using eight criteria across 12 district heating companies [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. The study’s sensitivity analysis varied criteria weights in three ways: changing them individually to determine stability ranges, changing them individually by a fixed amount to see effects on average scores, and comparing AHP weights with equal weights [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. Its main conclusion was that all five methods are suitable for sustainability analyses of district heating systems, but they differ in calculation process and in how results are interpreted [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. This indicates agreement on overall suitability while still highlighting methodological differences that can affect practical use [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. A related district-heating sustainability study used fuzzy AHP with fuzzy TOPSIS and reported that an 18-scenario sensitivity analysis supported the reliability and stability of the ranking results under changed sub-criteria weights [https://openalex.org/W4365453722||ABSTRACT||001]. Although that study did not compare multiple MCDA methods beyond the fuzzy AHP–fuzzy TOPSIS framework, it reinforces the broader finding that weight sensitivity is important for judging robustness in sustainability rankings [https://openalex.org/W4365453722||ABSTRACT||001]. Evidence from broader sustainability reviews also suggests growing use of hybrid MCDM approaches and ongoing concerns about subjective weight assignment and model uncertainty, which helps explain why sensitivity analysis is central in these assessments [https://openalex.org/W4407409800||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: A district heating sustainability study compared WSM, TOPSIS, PROMETHEE, ELECTRE, and DEA using eight criteria for 12 companies [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000].

Its sensitivity analysis tested weight changes by altering criteria individually, applying fixed changes, and comparing AHP weights with equal weights [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000].

The analysis concluded that all five methods are suitable for sustainability assessment of district heating systems, but they differ in calculation and interpretation [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000].

A separate district heating study using fuzzy AHP and fuzzy TOPSIS ran an 18-scenario sensitivity analysis to assess the reliability and stability of rankings under sub-criteria weight changes [https://openalex.org/W4365453722||ABSTRACT||001].

Broader sustainability reviews report increasing adoption of hybrid MCDM approaches and note challenges with subjective weight assignment and model uncertainty [https://openalex.org/W4407409800||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: Only one paper in the supplied evidence explicitly compares multiple MCDA methods for district heating systems, so the answer is based primarily on that single study [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000].

The evidence does not provide detailed numeric sensitivity results or step-by-step derivations showing exactly how each method differed in calculation or interpretation [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000].

One related district-heating paper used fuzzy AHP and fuzzy TOPSIS, but it did not compare a broader set of MCDA methods, limiting how far the findings can be generalized [https://openalex.org/W4365453722||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How do the sustainability ideas in the supply chain management framework and the article on sustainable marketing both show how environmental sustainability can be advanced and linked to company image?
draft_answer: Across the papers, sustainability is presented as something companies advance by embedding it into concrete business practices rather than treating it as a symbolic claim. In the supply chain management framework, environmental sustainability is strengthened through customer relationships, postponement, information sharing, and information quality, and these practices can also improve financial performance and help managers strengthen sustainability in manufacturing companies [https://openalex.org/W3132273715||ABSTRACT||001]. A related supply-chain/strategy perspective says sustainability becomes more effective when it is built into business strategy, where consumer, supplier, and employee engagement, reduced risk, and better operational management support broader company performance [https://openalex.org/W3135028795||ABSTRACT||002]. The more strategic supply-chain framework also argues that employees’ motivation and managerial attitude shape strategic sustainability orientation, which then works through corporate environmental management and corporate social responsibility to improve firm performance [https://openalex.org/W3128290205||ABSTRACT||000]. The sustainable marketing papers show a similar logic: companies advance environmental sustainability by reducing environmental impact, using sustainable practices, offering eco-friendly products, adapting marketing to consumer demands, and communicating sustainability transparently [https://openalex.org/W4383567484||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4396847081||ABSTRACT||000]. These marketing studies also make the company-image link explicit by showing that sustainability helps build customer trust, reputation, loyalty, competitive advantage, and stronger brand image [https://openalex.org/W4383567484||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4392716256||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4401289024||ABSTRACT||000]. One important contrast is that the supply-chain summaries emphasize operational and performance mechanisms, while the marketing summaries focus more directly on consumer perceptions, brand/reputation, and market differentiation [https://openalex.org/W3132273715||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3135028795||ABSTRACT||002] [https://openalex.org/W4383567484||ABSTRACT||001]. A further warning from the evidence is that sustainability must be implemented visibly: one paper reports that sustainability orientation can hurt brand image if it is not backed by action, creating greenwashing concerns, whereas actual implementation improves brand image [https://openalex.org/W4408946628||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the papers agree that environmental sustainability is advanced through concrete organizational practices and that company image improves when those practices are visible, credible, and tied to responsibility [https://openalex.org/W3128290205||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4408946628||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: The supply chain management framework advances environmental sustainability through customer relationships, postponement, information sharing, and information quality, while also improving financial performance [https://openalex.org/W3132273715||ABSTRACT||001].

Sustainable marketing advances environmental sustainability by reducing environmental impact, using sustainable practices, offering eco-friendly products, and adapting marketing to consumer demands with transparent communication [https://openalex.org/W4383567484||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4396847081||ABSTRACT||000].

Both the supply-chain and marketing evidence link sustainability to company image, but the supply-chain summaries do so mainly through corporate social responsibility and firm performance, while the marketing summaries do so through brand image, reputation, trust, and loyalty [https://openalex.org/W3128290205||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4383567484||ABSTRACT||001].

Embedding sustainability into business strategy can engage consumers, suppliers, and employees, reduce risk, and improve operational management and company performance [https://openalex.org/W3135028795||ABSTRACT||002].

Sustainability implementation is more important for brand image than orientation alone, because implementation positively mediates the orientation-brand image link and helps avoid greenwashing perceptions [https://openalex.org/W4408946628||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The evidence comes from summaries only, so the comparison is limited to the stated findings and mechanisms rather than full methods or detailed results.

The supply chain and marketing papers are not all directly comparable in scope, and some summaries emphasize operations while others emphasize consumer perception, so the link between the two frameworks is partly inferential.

One paper notes that sustainability orientation may hurt brand image if not backed by implementation, suggesting that the relationship between sustainability and company image can be negative when action is absent [https://openalex.org/W4408946628||ABSTRACT||000].
The provided evidence does not specify sample sizes, contexts, or geographic coverage for most papers, limiting confidence in how broadly the findings generalize.

query: How do sustainable technologies, such as clean energy in manufacturing and green and reverse logistics, support Industry 4.0 innovation and SDG-based growth in industrial enterprises, and what did the analysis find about enterprise adoption and environmental management?
draft_answer: Across the reviewed papers, sustainable technologies are consistently presented as enablers of Industry 4.0-driven innovation and SDG-oriented growth in industrial enterprises, especially when digital tools are linked to environmental goals [https://openalex.org/W4392974914||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000]. One review argues that Industry 4.0 applications can improve supply-chain optimization, traceability, waste reduction, and resource management, thereby reducing environmental impact and supporting a broader sustainability transition [https://openalex.org/W4392974914||ABSTRACT||000]. Another paper specifically connects clean energy in manufacturing and green/reverse logistics to Industry 4.0-enabled sustainable innovation, stating that these functions strengthen green process innovation capacity and the ability to develop or adopt sustainable technologies [https://openalex.org/W3189862204||ABSTRACT||000]. The Slovakia-based enterprise study provides empirical support for this linkage, reporting that more than 82% of 105 surveyed enterprises implement the SDGs and more than 70% prioritize environmental aspects in business management, with significant relationships found between environmental management in the context of SDGs and sustainability in production and logistics [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. It also found a statistically confirmed relationship between renewable energy technology use in industry and sustainability in logistics, which directly supports the query’s focus on clean energy and logistics-based sustainability [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the literature is not uniformly optimistic: one review notes negative environmental effects from Industry 4.0 systems, including air pollution, improper waste disposal, and excessive consumption of raw materials, information, and energy, suggesting a gap between intended and actual sustainable production [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence suggests that enterprise adoption of Industry 4.0 and sustainable technologies can improve environmental and organizational performance, but the benefits depend on how well firms integrate sustainability into management, logistics, and innovation practices [https://openalex.org/W4327944862||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||001].

key_claims.claim: Industry 4.0 technologies are repeatedly described as supporting sustainability and SDG-linked growth by improving environmental performance, innovation, and organizational processes [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000].

Clean energy in manufacturing and green/reverse logistics are presented as Industry 4.0-enabled sustainable innovation functions that strengthen green process innovation capacity [https://openalex.org/W3189862204||ABSTRACT||000].

In a Slovakian sample of 105 enterprises, more than 82% implemented the SDGs and more than 70% preferred environmental aspects in business management [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000].

The Slovakian analysis found significant relationships between environmental management in the context of SDGs and sustainability in production and logistics, and a statistically confirmed relationship between renewable energy technology use and sustainability in logistics [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000].

Some evidence also warns that Industry 4.0 can generate negative environmental effects, including air pollution, improper waste disposal, and excess consumption of raw materials, information, and energy [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: Several papers are literature reviews or conceptual studies, so their claims about sustainability are largely indirect rather than based on primary causal tests [https://openalex.org/W4392974914||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3170613256||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||000].

Evidence on enterprise adoption and environmental management is uneven: some papers report concrete adoption figures and management findings, while others explicitly do not provide such outcomes [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3189862204||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000].

The empirical adoption evidence is geographically limited, with one detailed study focused on 105 enterprises in Slovakia and another context-specific review centered on the UAE, so generalization across industrial sectors and regions remains uncertain [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How does the study use predictive analytics in the 1-hop work, and what does the 2-hop AI impact assessment say about AI"s role for sustainable development?
draft_answer: Across the supplied studies, the 1-hop work uses predictive analytics mainly as a forecasting and optimization tool: one paper says it forecasts future environmental impacts from historical data so companies can take proactive measures to reduce harm, while also using AI/ML/NLP to process heterogeneous inputs such as IoT sensors, satellite imagery, and corporate disclosures for environmental assessment and reporting [https://openalex.org/W4399702720||ABSTRACT||000]. Another paper describes predictive models and monitoring systems as improving resource monitoring, agricultural optimization, and waste management, and a third says deep learning and supervised machine learning are the most prominently applied algorithms for forecasting and system optimization in AI-related SDG research [https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4412514975||ABSTRACT||000]. One study further reports that an explainable AI predictive model outperforms traditional methods and supports sustainable energy management and Net Zero alignment, indicating that predictive analytics is being used not just for prediction but for practical sustainability decision support [https://openalex.org/W4404798080||ABSTRACT||000]. The 2-hop AI impact assessments are broadly optimistic about AI’s role for sustainable development, describing it as significant or transformative for sustainability, environmental accounting, urban development, and SDG implementation [https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4399702720||ABSTRACT||003; https://openalex.org/W4397008103||ABSTRACT||002]. Several papers emphasize that AI can provide data-driven insights, enhanced transparency, real-time monitoring, and environmental, economic, and social benefits, including climate mitigation and biodiversity support [https://openalex.org/W4412514975||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4399702720||ABSTRACT||003; https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the assessments are conditional rather than unconditional: they stress the need for supportive policies, infrastructure, continuous model refinement, interdisciplinary collaboration, and responsible governance to realize benefits [https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4399702720||ABSTRACT||003; https://openalex.org/W4414098400||ABSTRACT||000]. There is also some nuance in how strongly positive the 2-hop assessments are, ranging from strong consensus that AI positively affects most SDGs to more cautious framing that its full potential remains unrealized and that only a few studies combine advanced AI with deep sustainability expertise [https://openalex.org/W4396674183||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4412514975||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: In the 1-hop work, predictive analytics is used to forecast future environmental impacts from historical data so companies can take proactive measures, and AI/ML/NLP are used to process heterogeneous sustainability data from IoT sensors, satellite imagery, and corporate disclosures [https://openalex.org/W4399702720||ABSTRACT||000].

Predictive models and monitoring systems are described as improving resource monitoring, agricultural optimization, and waste management, while deep learning and supervised machine learning are highlighted as the main forecasting and optimization algorithms in AI-related SDG research [https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4412514975||ABSTRACT||000].

These assessments also say AI’s benefits depend on supportive policies, infrastructure, continuous refinement, interdisciplinary collaboration, and responsible governance [https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4399702720||ABSTRACT||003; https://openalex.org/W4414098400||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How are the SDOs linked to policy coherance for sustainable development in the EU context?
draft_answer: Across the reviewed papers, the SDGs are presented as an organizing framework for policy coherence for sustainable development in the EU, but not as a guarantee of coherent action [https://openalex.org/W4412423688||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4391173571||ABSTRACT||000]. Several studies describe coherence as essential to the 2030 Agenda because it helps ensure one goal is not achieved at the expense of another and because the Agenda explicitly calls for policy and institutional coherence [https://openalex.org/W4412423688||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000]. In the EU context, this coherence is linked to integrating SDGs into strategic frameworks for sustainable and inclusive growth and to using regional indicators and monitoring systems to align policies with local realities [https://openalex.org/W4399724167||ABSTRACT||000]. Evidence also suggests that SDG interactions matter empirically: EU countries’ progress is negatively associated with trade-offs and positively associated with synergies among indicators, implying that reducing conflicts and strengthening complementarities can improve coherence and progress [https://openalex.org/W4205096557||ABSTRACT||000]. However, multiple papers warn that coherence is limited by politics, institutions, and uneven uptake; one study argues that technocratic coordination can mask political struggles, while another finds SDG implementation is often patchy and sometimes symbolic [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4391173571||ABSTRACT||000]. The EU literature also identifies environmental goals as especially complex and least coherent, with calls to strengthen coherence within biodiversity and climate SDGs and improve data availability for monitoring [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, analytical tools such as LCA are described as pivotal for policy design and monitoring because they can strengthen EU policies toward the SDGs and planetary limits, although the interlinkages between policy, SDGs, and planetary boundaries are uneven across frameworks [https://openalex.org/W4210270578||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the papers agree that SDGs can support policy coherence in the EU only when they are backed by robust monitoring, multi-level and multi-actor integration, and attention to the political drivers of implementation rather than purely technical coordination [https://openalex.org/W4381802338||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4308113945||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: The SDGs are treated as a framework for policy coherence for sustainable development in the EU, but coherence is not automatic and depends on implementation conditions [https://openalex.org/W4412423688||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4391173571||ABSTRACT||000].

In the EU context, policy coherence is strengthened by integrating the SDGs into strategic governance and by using regional monitoring and indicators to align policies with sustainability goals [https://openalex.org/W4399724167||ABSTRACT||000].

EU countries’ SDG progress is negatively related to trade-offs and positively related to synergies among SDG indicators, showing that SDG interlinkages affect policy coherence and outcomes [https://openalex.org/W4205096557||ABSTRACT||000].

Environmental SDGs are described as the least coherent and most complex in the EU, making biodiversity and climate coherence a priority for improvement [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000].

Policy coherence for sustainable development depends on multi-level and multi-actor integration, including political leadership, horizontal integration, vertical integration, and stakeholder involvement [https://openalex.org/W4381802338||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The evidence is drawn from abstracts only, so the mechanisms and empirical details behind the claims are limited.
Several papers emphasize that coherence is uneven, symbolic, or politically constrained, so the extent to which SDGs improve EU policy coherence remains uncertain.
The summaries focus heavily on monitoring, integration, and governance design; they provide less direct evidence on concrete policy outcomes across all EU sectors.

query: How mask mandates help Covid-19 cases, and what did the study find?

One review says nano-enhancers with high thermal conductivity are recommended because they help solve the workpiece “burn puzzle,” especially for titanium alloy, and that high hardness and spherical characteristics are better because they improve grinding performance [https://openalex.org/W4313508734||ABSTRACT||001]. Another review describes nano-enhanced biolubricants as improving tribological, thermal, and machined-surface quality through advanced lubrication and heat transfer, with anti-friction effects and distinctive film formation, atomization, and infiltration mechanisms [https://openalex.org/W4206313494||ABSTRACT||000]. These papers agree that the appeal of nano-enhancers is largely their thermophysical and interfacial effects, which are framed as superior to conventional fluids for reducing wheel wear, surface burn, and tool wear [https://openalex.org/W4313508734||ABSTRACT||001][https://openalex.org/W4206313494||ABSTRACT||000]. A broader machining review also calls nanofluids an emerging technology because of their excellent thermophysical properties, but notes that alternative methods are not yet mature and that nanofluids remain developmental and need more detailed, cost-effective study [https://openalex.org/W4294292954||ABSTRACT||001]. At the same time, the evidence is not fully settled: one abstract emphasizes that the overall action of nano-enhanced biolubricants is still indistinct and depends on concentration and dispersion, so the benefits are not described as universal or fully understood [https://openalex.org/W4206313494||ABSTRACT||000]. Outside machining, related summaries only show that nanoparticles can improve material performance indirectly by improving microstructure or dispersion, but they do not directly explain workpiece burn behavior [https://pmc_PMC5512519||ABSTRACT||000][https://https://openalex.org/W4409451850||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How is the SDG Index used to measur progres toward the SDGs at local and regional level in Romania, and what did the results show?

A related Romania-focused study used the SDG Index in a simulation model to estimate how local and regional progress could evolve by 2030 and to identify a cost-effective path for each SDG in each city [https://openalex.org/W4285599931||ABSTRACT||001]. That simulation suggested that cities could achieve 9–13 more SDGs by 2030, and that the overall SDG Index could rise from 74.57 to 97.49 if more intensive path adjustment were adopted [https://openalex.org/W4285599931||ABSTRACT||001]. The Romanian local and regional results also showed strong spatial unevenness, with the highest sustainable development performances concentrated in specific geographical areas [https://openalex.org/W3135800278||ABSTRACT||000]. By contrast, rural areas and extended peripheral regions in the eastern and southern parts of Romania were the poorest performers [https://openalex.org/W3135800278||ABSTRACT||000]. More broadly, other papers in the set support the use of SDG-based composite or regional monitoring frameworks for benchmarking and localized assessment, emphasizing that such tools can reveal area-specific strengths and weaknesses and support tailored policy action [https://openalex.org/W4399724167||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4390511697||ABSTRACT||001]. At the same time, the evidence also suggests an important limitation of index-based monitoring: aggregate SDG index values can conceal divergent subregional trends, since an overall increase may hide declines in some subregions [https://openalex.org/W4206568419||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do sustainable technologies, such as clean energy in manufacturing and green and reverse logistics, support Industry 4.0 innovation and SDG-based growth in industrial enterprises, and what did the analysis find about enterprise adoption and environmental management?
draft_answer: Across the papers, sustainable technologies are consistently presented as enabling Industry 4.0-driven innovation and SDG-oriented growth by improving environmental sustainability, production efficiency, and organizational capabilities. Industry 4.0 is described as strengthening capabilities such as green absorptive capacity, sustainable partnership, and sustainable innovation orientation, which in turn support green process innovation and the development or reintroduction of eco-friendly products in an economical and competitive way [https://openalex.org/W3189862204||ABSTRACT||001]. A broader review likewise finds that Industry 4.0 technologies can improve environmental sustainability across production, supply chains, delivery chains, and market outcomes, and concludes that these technologies appear environmentally sustainable because they help manufacture goods more efficiently while reducing resource consumption [https://openalex.org/W4226256571||ABSTRACT||001]. More specifically, one study links sustainable technologies such as clean energy in manufacturing and green/reverse logistics with Industry 4.0 innovations and SDGs, finding significant relationships between green manufacturing, green logistics, reverse logistics, and technologies including autonomous robots, renewable energy, advanced materials, virtual technologies, and simulation [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||001]. That study also reports that more than 82% of the surveyed enterprises implement the SDGs and more than 70% prefer environmental aspects in business management, suggesting substantial enterprise uptake of sustainability-oriented practices in its Slovak sample [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. In line with this, the analysis found significant links between environmental management under the SDGs and sustainability in production and logistics, including renewable energy use, waste separation and recycling, environmental certification, environmental training, and continuous CO2 reduction in logistics activities [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||001]. At the same time, the literature is not uniformly optimistic: one review notes that Industry 4.0 and related technologies can also create negative environmental effects such as air pollution, improper waste disposal, and excessive use of raw materials, information, and energy, and it identifies a gap between current and intended sustainable production conditions [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||000]. Other reviews reinforce the SDG connection by showing that Industry 4.0 supports circular economy practices and links them to SDGs such as clean energy, responsible consumption and production, and climate action, while also proposing frameworks for organizational realignment rather than reporting direct adoption outcomes [https://openalex.org/W4210290448||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence suggests that sustainable technologies support Industry 4.0 innovation and SDG-based growth through cleaner, more efficient, and more circular production and logistics systems, but adoption appears uneven and several studies emphasize barriers, early-stage development, or the need for further research and implementation guidance [https://openalex.org/W4288738282||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3173460341||ABSTRACT||001].

key_claims.claim: Industry 4.0 can strengthen capabilities such as green absorptive capacity, sustainable partnership, and sustainable innovation orientation, which support green process innovation and the development or reintroduction of eco-friendly products [https://openalex.org/W3189862204||ABSTRACT||001].

A review found that Industry 4.0 technologies can improve environmental sustainability across production, supply chains, delivery chains, and market outcomes by enabling more efficient manufacturing and lower resource consumption [https://openalex.org/W4226256571||ABSTRACT||001].

Clean energy in manufacturing and green/reverse logistics were found to have significant relationships with selected Industry 4.0 technologies, including autonomous robots, renewable energy, advanced materials, virtual technologies, and simulation [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||001].

In the Slovak enterprise sample, more than 82% of surveyed enterprises implement the SDGs and more than 70% prefer environmental aspects in business management [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000].

Environmental management under the SDGs was significantly linked to sustainability in production and logistics, including renewable energy use, waste separation and recycling, environmental certification, environmental training, and continuous CO2 reduction in logistics activities [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||001].

Some literature also reports negative environmental effects from Industry 4.0 and related technologies, including air pollution, improper waste disposal, and excessive use of raw materials, information, and energy [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: Several papers are broad literature reviews or conceptual frameworks and do not report direct enterprise-level causal effects of specific sustainable technologies on innovation or environmental performance [https://openalex.org/W4210290448||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||001].

Evidence on adoption is uneven: one study provides enterprise percentages from Slovakia, but other papers explicitly note that they do not report adoption rates or detailed environmental management outcomes [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4210290448||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4288738282||ABSTRACT||001].

Some findings are context-specific or early-stage, such as warehouse management research described as still at an early stage and affected by barriers like weak government support, legal issues, lack of skilled manpower, political issues, and old warehouses [https://openalex.org/W4288738282||ABSTRACT||001].

The papers do not provide a single unified empirical assessment of clean energy in manufacturing and green/reverse logistics across sectors and regions, so generalization beyond the reported samples and reviews is limited [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How are the SDOs linked to policy coherance for sustainable development in the EU context?
draft_answer: Across the EU-focused papers, the SDGs are consistently presented as a framework for policy coherence for sustainable development, meaning that policies should be aligned so progress on one goal does not undermine others [W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000][W4412423688||ABSTRACT||000]. Several studies treat this coherence as a practical coordination problem: one paper maps Country-Specific Recommendations, the SDGs, and the European Green Deal to help the EU Commission and Member States better align policy priorities with the sustainability agenda, while another frames the circular economy as a way to assess whether SDG fulfilment and EU implementation outcomes align across member states [W3194602120||ABSTRACT||001][W3209532954||ABSTRACT||000]. The European Green Deal is repeatedly described as a key policy arena where SDGs can be operationalized, with one study finding strong alignment with SDG7, SDG13, and SDG12 but weak alignment with social SDGs, showing that coherence is uneven rather than comprehensive [W4392741850||ABSTRACT||000]. Other work similarly finds that the EU has generally incorporated the SDGs into its strategic priorities, but that important challenges identified in the Sustainable Development Report 2020 were not captured by the CSRs, indicating gaps in policy coverage [W3194602120||ABSTRACT||001]. The literature also points to sectoral pathways for coherence, such as Goal 9 for infrastructure, industry, and innovation, and SDG 7, where coherent economic policy, government collaboration, and supportive financial regulation are presented as necessary levers [W4362550191||ABSTRACT||000][W4402759895||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the evidence suggests that coherence is not purely technical: one paper argues that SDG-based institutional arrangements can create an apolitical façade that may limit transformative change, and another notes that the coherence framing depends on technical fixes for issues that are fundamentally political [W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000][W4412423688||ABSTRACT||000]. Methods-oriented papers further suggest that tools such as LCA can support EU policy design and monitoring, but the interlinkages among LCA, EU policy, the SDGs, and planetary boundaries are mixed, with some links existing, some missing, and some dependent on the framework used [W4210270578||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence indicates that in the EU context the SDGs are linked to policy coherence through alignment exercises, cross-sector coordination, and monitoring tools, but also that major social and environmental gaps, weak interlinkages, and political tensions remain [W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000][W4366975340||ABSTRACT||001][W4392741850||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: In the EU context, the SDGs are used as a framework for policy coherence for sustainable development, emphasizing that policies should be aligned so progress on one goal does not undermine others [W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000][W4412423688||ABSTRACT||000].

The EU has generally incorporated the SDGs into its strategic priorities, but important sustainability challenges were not captured by the Country-Specific Recommendations, indicating gaps in coherence [W3194602120||ABSTRACT||001].
The European Green Deal shows uneven coherence with the SDGs, with strong alignment to SDG7, SDG13, and SDG12 but weak alignment to several social SDGs [W4392741850||ABSTRACT||000].

Goal 9 and Goal 7 are presented as specific policy levers for coherence because they require coordinated action across infrastructure, industry, innovation, economic policy, and financial regulation [W4362550191||ABSTRACT||000][W4402759895||ABSTRACT||000].

Policy coherence is not only technical but also political, because SDG-based institutional arrangements may create an apolitical façade and technical fixes may fail to address structural tensions [W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000][W4412423688||ABSTRACT||000].

The literature identifies analytical tools such as LCA and 3D-mapping as ways to support EU policy design, monitoring, and alignment across sustainability frameworks [W4210270578||ABSTRACT||000][W3194602120||ABSTRACT||001].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The evidence is drawn from abstracts only, so several papers provide limited methodological detail and no full-text assessment of how coherence is measured or operationalized.

Findings are uneven across policy domains: social SDGs appear underrepresented in the European Green Deal, while environmental and energy-related goals receive more attention [W4392741850||ABSTRACT||000].

Some papers explicitly note that the coherence framing is politically contested or only implicit, so the relationship between SDGs and policy coherence is not described uniformly across studies [W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000][W4412423688||ABSTRACT||000].

Several studies are context-specific, including analyses of the Netherlands or sectoral focus areas such as circular economy, Goal 7, and Goal 9, which limits how far the conclusions can be generalized across all EU policy areas [W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000][W3209532954||ABSTRACT||000][W4362550191||ABSTRACT||000].

query: What did the interviews with retailers and service providers in North America reveal about managing product returns sustainably?
draft_answer: The interviews with multichannel retailers, retail experts, and return service providers in the UK and North America found that retailers were paying attention to the financial impact of returns, but they had little awareness of the environmental scale of returns and no comprehensive approach to managing that impact sustainably [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||001]. The evidence suggests a gap between recognizing returns as a business cost and treating them as a sustainability issue, because retailers focused on financial consequences rather than environmental ones [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||000]. Another study indicates that sustainable practice can be undermined by paradoxes, implying that return management should avoid actions that create conflicting outcomes [https://openalex.org/W3135380255||ABSTRACT||001]. Consistent with that, the same paper urges retailers to move toward cradle-to-cradle, closed-loop lifecycle supply chains and to evaluate whether adopted practices actually support sustainability goals [https://openalex.org/W3135380255||ABSTRACT||001]. It also emphasizes considering the whole supply chain and the role of each actor when implementing sustainable practices, which aligns with the need for coordinated returns management across retailers and service providers [https://openalex.org/W3135380255||ABSTRACT||001]. The paper on returns management further concludes that retailers face barriers to developing environmental sustainability plans and proposes strategies and a framework to reduce the environmental impact of product returns [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the interviews reveal an emerging awareness of returns as a sustainability problem, but one that is still underdeveloped in practice and in need of clearer frameworks, supply-chain coordination, and more holistic planning [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3135380255||ABSTRACT||001].

key_claims.claim: Retailers interviewed in the UK and North America were aware of the financial impact of product returns but had little awareness of their environmental scale [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||001].

The interviews found no comprehensive approach to managing product returns sustainably, and retailers faced barriers to developing environmental sustainability plans for returns management [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||001].

The returns-management paper proposes strategies and a framework to reduce the environmental impact of product returns [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||001].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The evidence is limited to interview-based findings summarized in abstracts, so it does not provide detailed methods, sample sizes, or the specific strategies discussed.
The returns-management findings combine the UK and North America, so the evidence does not isolate North American interview results on their own.

query: How are coronary artery calcifications associated with complications?
draft_answer: Across the supplied studies, coronary artery calcification is consistently associated with worse outcomes, but the type of complication differs by population and setting. In symptomatic patients referred for cardiac CT, higher coronary artery calcium score was associated with all-cause mortality over 4.4 years, with only modest discrimination for prognosis [pmc_PMC9806039||ABSTRACT||000]. In level-1 trauma patients, left main coronary artery calcification was independently associated with any complication (OR 3.9, 95% CI 1.7–8.9) and with adverse discharge condition, and a greater number of calcified coronary arteries showed a trend toward more complications [pmc_PMC10229702||ABSTRACT||001]. In heavily calcified coronary lesions treated with orbital atherectomy, the calcification burden was substantial and was associated with the need for invasive imaging and plaque modification, including superficial sanding in 90% of vessels and fracturing of deeper medial calcium in 63% of vessels [pmc_PMC10140256||ABSTRACT||000]. Despite that procedural complexity, the atherectomy series reported 66% device success, 94% procedural success, and no primary safety events during 30 days of follow-up [pmc_PMC10140256||ABSTRACT||001]. Broader cardiovascular literature in the summaries also indicates that CAC predicts future ASCVD risk independent of conventional risk factors and improves risk prediction when added to the Framingham risk score [pmc_PMC5383538||ABSTRACT||000]. However, the summaries also show important limits: no clinical trial has shown that CAC screening improves clinical outcomes or healthcare costs, and similar CAC levels may correspond to different absolute risks across regions and ethnic groups [pmc_PMC5383538||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence supports CAC as a marker of higher risk for mortality, in-hospital complications, and greater procedural complexity, but not as a proven intervention target that itself has established outcome benefit [pmc_PMC9806039||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10229702||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC10140256||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC5383538||ABSTRACT||000].
