query: How does the combined detecion of KAI1 and VEGF improve the diagnosis of HCC?
draft_answer: Combined detection of KAI1 and VEGF appears to improve HCC diagnosis by leveraging two markers with opposite expression patterns in patients with HCC: serum KAI1 is downregulated, while VEGF is upregulated [pmc_PMC4164248||ABSTRACT||000]. In the same study, KAI1 was associated with TNM staging, intrahepatic metastasis, lymph node/peritoneal metastasis, and portal vein thrombus, while VEGF was closely related to alpha-fetoprotein level, suggesting that the two markers may capture different clinically relevant aspects of disease [pmc_PMC4164248||ABSTRACT||000]. Diagnostic performance was better when both markers were used together than when either was used alone, with sensitivity increasing from 86.96% to 91.86%, accuracy from 83.06% to 84.68%, and negative predictive value to 78.79% [pmc_PMC4164248||ABSTRACT||001]. query: How mask mandates help Covid-19 cases, and what did the study find?

A separate study found that keeping face mask mandates in place for at least two months, rather than less than one month, was associated with lower COVID-19 incidence, with reductions ranging from 4 fewer cases per 100,000 in low-social-vulnerability counties to 401 fewer cases per 100,000 in high-social-vulnerability counties [pmc_PMC9729715||ABSTRACT||001]. However, one ventilation-focused study cautioned that masks can be counterproductive if used inappropriately with ventilation, suggesting that mask policies work best when combined with proper environmental controls [pmc_PMC9803700||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the evidence in these summaries supports mask mandates as a useful non-pharmaceutical intervention for reducing COVID-19 spread, but the magnitude of benefit appears to depend on compliance, duration, and context [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9729715||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC9803700||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How do sustainable technologies, such as clean energy in manufacturing and green and reverse logistics, support Industry 4.0 innovation and SDG-based growth in industrial enterprises, and what did the analysis find about enterprise adoption and environmental management?
draft_answer: Across the papers, sustainable technologies are consistently presented as enabling Industry 4.0 innovation by improving efficiency, reducing resource consumption, and strengthening environmental performance in manufacturing and supply chains [https://openalex.org/W4226256571||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||001]. The clearest specific evidence comes from the study on clean energy in manufacturing and green/reverse logistics, which argues that these technologies create conditions for industrial development and future growth when combined with Industry 4.0 and SDG-oriented innovation [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. That same study also reports that, among 105 Slovak enterprises, more than 82% said they implemented the SDGs and more than 70% preferred environmental aspects in business management, with a significant relationship between environmental management under the SDGs and sustainability in production and logistics [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. It further found a statistically confirmed relationship between renewable energy technology use in industry and sustainability in logistics, reinforcing the link between sustainable technologies and SDG-based growth in industrial enterprises [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. More broadly, multiple reviews agree that Industry 4.0 supports sustainability and corporate growth, with reported benefits including better environmental performance, ecological support, and reduced environmental impact [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4311719782||ABSTRACT||000]. The literature also frames this as a pathway toward Sustainability 4.0, where digitisation helps preserve energy and natural resources while contributing to a more socially inclusive and environmentally sustainable economy [https://openalex.org/W4282842216||ABSTRACT||001]. At the same time, the evidence is uneven: several papers offer only general Industry 4.0–sustainability claims without specific findings on clean energy, green/reverse logistics, adoption rates, or environmental management outcomes [https://openalex.org/W4392974914||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3170613256||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000]. Adoption also appears context-dependent, since one study notes stronger sustainability adoption in developed economies with strong infrastructure and limited adoption in emerging economies [https://openalex.org/W3120619572||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the synthesis suggests that sustainable technologies and Industry 4.0 are mutually reinforcing, but the most concrete enterprise-level evidence is still concentrated in a single country case with limited detail on broader environmental management mechanisms [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4282842216||ABSTRACT||001].

key_claims.claim: Sustainable technologies such as clean energy in manufacturing and green/reverse logistics are described as creating conditions for industrial development and future growth when combined with Industry 4.0 and SDG-oriented innovation [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000].

In the 2-hop AI impact assessments, AI is generally framed as important for sustainable development because it can enable data-driven insights, optimizations, and solutions to environmental and SDG-related challenges [https://openalex.org/W4412514975||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4392169541||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4405499395||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the synthesis suggests that predictive analytics is one of the concrete mechanisms through which AI contributes to sustainability, while the 2-hop assessments portray AI’s role for sustainable development as promising but conditional, context-dependent, and in need of careful evaluation and governance [https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4412514975||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3135629427||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How are the SDOs linked to policy coherance for sustainable development in the EU context?
draft_answer: Across the papers, the SDGs are presented as a central framework for assessing and steering policy coherence for sustainable development in the EU, because they make it possible to track environmental, social, and economic dimensions together rather than separately [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000]. Several studies show that coherence is pursued by aligning EU strategies and instruments with the SDGs, including the European Green Deal, the Country-Specific Recommendations in the European Semester, circular economy policy, and Life Cycle Assessment as a monitoring and design tool [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W3209532954||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4210270578||ABSTRACT||000]. The literature also suggests that the SDGs help identify where coherence is weakest: environmental SDGs are described as the most complex and least coherent, while interlinkages among EU policies, the SDGs, and planetary boundaries can be “existing, missing, or existing depending on the LCA framework” [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4210270578||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, coherence is not treated as purely technical, since one paper argues that policy coherence for sustainable development is shaped by political drivers such as ideas, institutions, and interests, and that technical arrangements may create an apolitical façade that limits transformative change [https://openalex.org/W4308113945||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000]. Other papers reinforce this by recommending system perspectives, attention to trade-offs, and context-specific priorities across governance levels and scales of implementation [https://openalex.org/W4366975340||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the papers agree that the SDGs support policy coherence by providing a common reference point for alignment, monitoring, and comparison across EU policies and member states, but they also show that coherence remains incomplete and uneven, especially where political trade-offs, weak intra-cluster links, or missing policy coverage persist [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||001; https://openalex.org/W4366975340||ABSTRACT||001; https://openalex.org/W4312225363||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: In the EU context, the SDGs serve as a framework for tracking sustainability across environmental, social, and economic dimensions, making policy coherence a central challenge [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000].

EU policy coherence is linked to the SDGs through efforts to align the European Green Deal, the European Semester/CSRs, circular economy policy, and Life Cycle Assessment with sustainable development objectives [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W3209532954||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4210270578||ABSTRACT||000].

The papers describe environmental SDGs as among the least coherent areas and emphasize improving data availability and monitoring, especially for biodiversity and climate-related SDGs [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000].

Policy coherence for sustainable development is presented as political as well as technical, shaped by ideas, institutions, and interests rather than by neutral coordination alone [https://openalex.org/W4308113945||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000].

The evidence suggests that EU SDG implementation and coherence vary across countries and policy areas, with some goals and recommendations not fully captured in existing coordination processes [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||001; https://openalex.org/W4312225363||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The evidence is mostly abstract-level and does not provide detailed mechanisms or quantitative estimates of how much coherence improves when SDGs are used.
Several findings are context-specific, including a Netherlands case and member-state rankings, so generalization across the entire EU should be cautious.
Some papers note gaps in coverage or weak intra-cluster connections, but the summaries do not specify which policy instruments are most effective in fixing these gaps.
The evidence includes both technocratic and political interpretations of coherence, indicating unresolved tension over whether coordination alone can deliver transformative change.

query: How do the themes of "Environmental sustainability", "Sustainability implementation barriers", and "Sustainable residential buildings" connect when comparing off-site construction research with the barrier analysis in Ghana and the "Mostadam" approach in Saudi Arabia, and what sustainability-related findings are highlighted across these contexts?
draft_answer: Across the provided studies, the three themes connect through a shared concern with how environmental sustainability is translated into building practice, especially for residential and affordable housing [https://openalex.org/W3168941981||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4386401188||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3120903819||ABSTRACT||001]. Taken together, the evidence suggests a consistent pattern: sustainable residential buildings are not only about design or rating systems, but also about the barriers, indicators, and implementation conditions that determine whether sustainability can actually be achieved [https://openalex.org/W3120903819||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3168941981||ABSTRACT||000]. At the local level, the city-level simulation suggested that the SDG Index can be used not only to score current performance but also to identify city-specific routes for improving all SDGs jointly by 2030 [https://openalex.org/W4285599931||ABSTRACT||001]. At the regional level, related SDG-based monitoring work indicates that the framework can support benchmarking and help isolate environmental indicators to reveal areas needing improvement and to assess how policy frameworks contribute to environmental progress [https://openalex.org/W4390511697||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4399724167||ABSTRACT||001]. The Romanian SDG Index results showed a highly uneven spatial pattern, with the strongest sustainable development performance concentrated in specific geographical areas [https://openalex.org/W3135800278||ABSTRACT||000]. By contrast, rural areas and extended peripheral regions in eastern and southern Romania were the poorest performers, indicating that progress was not evenly distributed across the country [https://openalex.org/W3135800278||ABSTRACT||000]. In the city-level modeling, the index suggested substantial room for improvement: 75.79% of cities could achieve 9–13 more SDGs by 2030, and the overall SDG index could increase from 74.57 to 97.49 under more intensive path adjustment [https://openalex.org/W4285599931||ABSTRACT||001]. Other papers in the set support the broader idea that SDG indicators are useful for regional benchmarking and policy guidance, but they do not provide Romania-specific SDG Index results [https://openalex.org/W4399724167||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4206568419||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence suggests that the SDG Index is being used in Romania to identify spatial disparities, benchmark local and regional performance, and model improvement pathways, with the main finding being that development is concentrated in some areas while rural and peripheral eastern and southern regions lag behind [https://openalex.org/W3135800278||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4285599931||ABSTRACT||001].

The SDG Index results in Romania showed that the highest sustainable development performance was concentrated in specific geographical areas, while rural areas and extended peripheral regions in eastern and southern Romania were the poorest performers [https://openalex.org/W3135800278||ABSTRACT||000].

In Romanian cities, the SDG Index simulation suggested that 75.79% of cities could achieve 9–13 more SDGs by 2030, and the overall SDG index could rise from 74.57 to 97.49 with more intensive path adjustment [https://openalex.org/W4285599931||ABSTRACT||001].

Related regional SDG framework papers emphasize benchmarking, environmental indicator selection, and policy alignment, but they do not provide Romania-specific SDG Index results [https://openalex.org/W4390511697||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4399724167||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How FT's do they add their own personal interpretation to sustainability requirements when they fulfill their boundary-spanning role?
draft_answer: The evidence shows that whether FTs add their own personal interpretation to sustainability requirements depends on the specific setting and how the boundary-spanning role is framed. One paper explicitly states that FTs do add their own personal interpretation when fulfilling their boundary-spanning role, and distinguishes between compliance-oriented and improvement-oriented boundary-spanning actions [https://openalex.org/W3205987731||ABSTRACT||001]. Relatedly, a study of sustainability managers finds that boundary-spanning is enabled by individual values, multidisciplinary knowledge, and relational abilities, and that responses to conflicting sustainability and profitability goals are shaped by contextual forces and individual cognitive characteristics [https://openalex.org/W4390583545||ABSTRACT||000]. Another paper similarly argues that professionals do not interpret sustainability requirements uniformly, but instead operationalise sustainability integration in ways that vary across professional and geographical contexts, leaving room for subjective understanding [https://openalex.org/W4313908265||ABSTRACT||000]. However, several other papers do not support a personal-reinterpretation reading and instead describe boundary-spanning or sustainability work in more general or structural terms, such as linking internal activities to environmental performance, responding to multi-level regulations and standards, or incorporating diverse perspectives through intentional practices [https://openalex.org/W3157489939||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4205454498||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4382811259||ABSTRACT||001]. Likewise, one paper on sustainability reporting notes that actors have diverse objectives and cannot give up their own perspectives, which suggests interpretation differences among boundary-spanners, while another says sustainability standards are shaped to serve state and industrial interests rather than being individually reinterpreted by FTs [https://openalex.org/W4225388860||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4313644972||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the literature implies that personal interpretation can matter in boundary-spanning sustainability work, but it is not consistently theorized or observed across all studies, and in many cases the focus is instead on institutional design, governance context, or intentional inclusion of diverse perspectives [https://openalex.org/W4304687713||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3216416295||ABSTRACT||001].

Several studies instead frame sustainability work in structural or intentional terms rather than as individual reinterpretation by FTs [https://openalex.org/W3157489939||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4205454498||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4382811259||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How does organizational learning capability contribute to radical innovation?

The clearest radical-innovation finding is that organizational learning capability fully mediates the relationship between stewardship leader behavior and radical innovation, meaning it is the pathway through which leadership supports radical innovation [https://openalex.org/W3194620278||ABSTRACT||000]. That same study describes organizational learning capability as a context that promotes experimentation, dialog, participative decision-making, risk-taking, and external interaction, which are all presented as mechanisms that boost radical innovation [https://openalex.org/W3194620278||ABSTRACT||000]. Other studies reinforce the broader idea that learning capabilities improve downstream outcomes: organizational learning positively influences sustainable value creation and is strengthened by stakeholder engagement, while innovation capability also serves as an intermediate capability in that pathway [https://openalex.org/W4400127182||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4400127182||ABSTRACT||001]. Similarly, organizational learning is described as important for sustainable organizational performance and as making innovation more informed and less disruptive when it is well-processed [https://openalex.org/W4378746192||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4378746192||ABSTRACT||001]. Additional papers support the broader pattern that learning-related capabilities help organizations adapt to new phenomena, such as sustainability, and improve performance, even when they do not address radical innovation directly [https://openalex.org/W4393229185||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W3211385979||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the evidence suggests that organizational learning capability contributes to radical innovation by creating an organizational environment that supports experimentation, learning from the external environment, and the translation of leadership or stakeholder inputs into innovative action, but most studies stop at related outcomes rather than directly testing radical innovation [https://openalex.org/W3194620278||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4400127182||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4406044302||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How does global public health get threat from microplastics in fishmeal?
draft_answer: The strongest direct evidence in these summaries is that microplastics can enter aquaculture through contaminated fishmeal or commercial fish feed, creating a pathway into fish raised for human consumption [https://openalex.org/W4388496957||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4282929872||ABSTRACT||000]. In Bangladesh, commercial fish feeds were reported as fully contaminated with microplastics at mean levels of 500–2200 MPs/kg, which the study framed as a global public health concern because many developing countries rely on aquaculture fish for protein [https://openalex.org/W4388496957||ABSTRACT||000]. Another paper similarly states that microplastics in fishmeal may interact with pond ecosystems, alter cultured fish physiology and behavior, and accumulate in edible portions of fish, potentially causing severe physiological disorders in consumers [https://openalex.org/W4282929872||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4282929872||ABSTRACT||001]. Several papers broaden this concern by noting that microplastics can persist, carry hazardous chemicals such as persistent organic pollutants, and act as a pathway for harmful contaminants through the food chain, with consequences for human health [https://openalex.org/W4408578227||ABSTRACT||000]. However, the evidence also shows uncertainty: one zebrafish study found no serious toxic effects from tested polyethylene microplastics because there was no internalization, although some biochemical markers changed [https://pmc_PMC9967563||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the summaries agree that the main public-health threat from microplastics in fishmeal is indirect exposure via contaminated farmed fish and potential food-chain contamination, but they do not provide direct human epidemiological evidence or a full mechanism for health outcomes [https://openalex.org/W4388496957||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4282929872||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4408578227||ABSTRACT||000].

query: What clinical and laboratory findings are associated with elevated FSH in men with non-obstructive azoospermia and chromosomal anomalies, and how do KS and testicular XX DSD compare with the undefined cause group?
draft_answer: In men with non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA) and chromosomal anomalies, elevated FSH is linked to a more impaired testicular and clinical profile, including smaller testicular volume and severe sperm-production failure. One study found that in men with chromosomal anomalies, KS was associated with elevated FSH together with lower mean testicular volume, shorter penile length, lower total testosterone, higher LH, greater height and arm span, and more frequent gynecomastia [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001]. The same study reported that testicular XX DSD showed LH and FSH values intermediate between KS and the undefined-cause group, with penile length also intermediate, testicular volume similar to KS, and other data similar to the undefined-cause group [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001]. Another study similarly found that high FSH was common in KS and testicular XX DSD, with 90.9% of KS and 100% of testicular XX DSD cases showing high FSH versus 66.7% in the undefined-cause group [pmc_PMC10307663||ABSTRACT||000]. In that study, elevated-FSH cases with chromosomal abnormalities usually had small or mildly reduced testicular volume, and azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia was present in the evaluated patients [pmc_PMC10307663||ABSTRACT||000]. Across these reports, KS appears more consistently associated with a broader hypogonadal phenotype, whereas testicular XX DSD is more variable and often intermediate between KS and undefined causes [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001][pmc_PMC10307663||ABSTRACT||000]. A separate NOA cohort also found that failed sperm retrieval was associated with elevated serum FSH and LH, while successful retrieval was associated with larger testicular volume and a higher testosterone/LH ratio, supporting FSH as part of a broader marker set for poor spermatogenic outcomes [pmc_PMC10307674||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC10307674||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the evidence suggests that elevated FSH in NOA with chromosomal anomalies tracks with reduced testicular volume and more severe reproductive endocrine abnormalities, and that KS tends to be more abnormal than the undefined-cause group, while testicular XX DSD is partly intermediate and partly similar to undefined-cause cases [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001][pmc_PMC10307663||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How is the translational regulation of NEDD4 linked to the IGF1 signaling pathway, and what does the context say about NEDD4 in cells that depend on this pathway?

In that study, NEDD4 knockdown suppressed growth and overexpression promoted it in IGF1R-dependent gastric cancer cells, while IGF1R-independent cells did not respond to either manipulation [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001]. This indicates that NEDD4’s effect is context-dependent and is tied to dependence on IGF1/IGF1R signaling rather than being universal across gastric cancer cells [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001]. The clinical context also supports this association, because NEDD4 is higher in IGF1-high gastric cancer tissues than in IGF1-low or normal tissues, and co-high NEDD4/IGF1 expression predicts worse prognosis [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001]. Other supplied papers do not provide evidence for an IGF1 link; one instead reports translational upregulation of NEDD4 in PDAC cells and connects it to PTEN/PI3K/AKT signaling, not IGF1 [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||000]. Additional papers mention no NEDD4/IGF1 relationship and focus on unrelated pathways, such as TGFβ1/Smad4, eIF3i in angiogenesis, or Nedd4-2 in PDD-related glutamate transporter regulation [pmc_PMC5386959||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC5386737||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC5386455||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC5386455||ABSTRACT||001]. For example, one paper describes “advanced predictive models and monitoring systems” for better resource monitoring, climate-change mitigation, and biodiversity promotion, while another links predictive analytics with cleaner production to optimize resources, reduce carbon footprint, and eliminate waste across industries [https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4402735735||ABSTRACT||000]. A further study says AI supports real-time data analysis, predictive modeling, and optimization in environmental science, including environmental monitoring, climate-change prediction, conservation, biodiversity, and sustainable resource management [https://openalex.org/W4392169541||ABSTRACT||000]. More broadly, the literature on SDG-related research shows deep learning and supervised machine learning are prominent for forecasting and system optimization, although only a few studies combine advanced AI applications with deep sustainability expertise [https://openalex.org/W4412514975||ABSTRACT||000]. The 2-hop impact assessments are consistent in portraying AI as broadly beneficial for sustainable development, with significant potential across environmental, economic, and social dimensions [https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4402735735||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers specify that AI can help achieve sustainability goals through lower energy and material use, better waste handling, better resource efficiency, and support for SDGs or net-zero-related goals [https://openalex.org/W4402735735||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400261689||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4405499395||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the evidence repeatedly notes that AI’s benefits are conditional on supportive policies, infrastructure, regulation, data quality, and explainability, and that high costs, privacy concerns, technical skill needs, and social resistance can limit impact [https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400261689||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4401830906||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400261689||ABSTRACT||000]. Expert and review-based assessments are also optimistic: one Delphi study reports an overall positive role for AI in sustainable development with especially positive impacts for SDGs 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 13, 14, and 15, while Goals 16 and 17 are neutral [https://openalex.org/W4396674183||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the papers agree that AI is being used as a forecasting and optimization tool in the 1-hop work and is seen in the 2-hop assessments as a central enabler of sustainable development, but one whose real-world value depends on governance, infrastructure, and interdisciplinary implementation [https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4412514975||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4392169541||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: In the 1-hop work, predictive analytics appears as part of AI-driven monitoring, forecasting, and optimization for sustainability, including resource monitoring, climate-change mitigation, biodiversity promotion, cleaner production, and environmental prediction [https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4402735735||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4392169541||ABSTRACT||000].

The 2-hop AI impact assessments generally describe AI as having a positive or significant role in sustainable development across environmental, economic, and social dimensions [https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4402735735||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4396674183||ABSTRACT||000].

Several studies say AI can help achieve SDGs or sustainability goals by improving resource efficiency, waste management, emissions reduction, and environmental outcomes such as net-zero-related objectives [https://openalex.org/W4400261689||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4402735735||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4405499395||ABSTRACT||000].

The evidence also stresses that AI’s sustainability benefits depend on supportive policies, infrastructure, regulation, data quality, explainability, and training, with barriers including high costs, privacy concerns, technical skill gaps, and social resistance [https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400261689||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4401830906||ABSTRACT||000].

One Delphi study reports an overall positive AI role in sustainable development with a robust mean score of 78.8%, especially positive for SDGs 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 13, 14, and 15, while SDGs 16 and 17 are neutral [https://openalex.org/W4396674183||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How are the SDOs linked to policy coherance for sustainable development in the EU context?
draft_answer: Across the EU literature, the SDGs are consistently presented as a framework for policy coherence because they connect environmental, social, and economic objectives into a single sustainability agenda [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers argue that coherence is achieved by aligning EU policy instruments and governance layers, including the Green Deal, European Semester CSRs, recovery planning, and national priorities, so that policies reinforce rather than undermine one another [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4210270578||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the evidence suggests that this coherence is uneven in practice: environmental goals are described as the most complex and least coherent SDGs in the EU, with biodiversity and climate needing stronger monitoring and data [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000]. The literature also emphasizes that policy coherence requires attention to territorial diversity, because EU-wide monitoring should be localized and customized to capture different regional progress and challenges [https://openalex.org/W4399724167||ABSTRACT||000]. Tool-based approaches such as Life Cycle Assessment, circular economy analysis, and regional indicator sets are presented as ways to support coherence by improving policy design, monitoring, and comparability across contexts [https://openalex.org/W4210270578||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4399724167||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3209532954||ABSTRACT||000]. However, one paper warns that the SDG framing can create an apolitical façade: technical and “win-win” solutions may obscure genuinely political incoherencies and limit transformative change [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000]. More broadly, the EU research landscape is said to have poor intra-cluster connections and a need for more transdisciplinary and system-level research that explicitly addresses trade-offs and context-specific priorities [https://openalex.org/W4366975340||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the papers agree that SDGs are used as a coordinating reference for sustainable development policy in the EU, but they differ on whether current institutional and analytical arrangements are sufficient to deliver truly transformative coherence [https://openalex.org/W4362550191||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4402759895||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: In the EU context, the SDGs function as a common framework for linking environmental, social, and economic goals and for improving policy coherence across sustainability policy [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000].

EU policy coherence for sustainable development is often operationalized by aligning the SDGs with the Green Deal, the European Semester CSRs, and recovery planning so that policy priorities remain consistent across levels [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||001].

The literature identifies environmental SDGs, especially biodiversity and climate, as the least coherent and most complex in the EU, indicating a need for better data and monitoring [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000].

Policy coherence also depends on recognizing regional differences, because localized monitoring and customized indicators are needed to reflect diverse territorial challenges across Europe [https://openalex.org/W4399724167||ABSTRACT||000].

Analytical tools such as Life Cycle Assessment and circular economy frameworks are presented as mechanisms that can strengthen SDG-related policy coherence by supporting design and monitoring [https://openalex.org/W4210270578||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3209532954||ABSTRACT||000].

A major tension in the literature is that the SDG framing may mask political incoherencies by presenting them as technical “win-win” issues, which can constrain transformative sustainability policy change [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000].

limitations_and_uncertainty: The summaries are based on abstracts, so they provide limited detail on methods, effect sizes, or the strength of empirical evidence.
Several papers emphasize tools and frameworks for coherence, but the summaries do not show whether these approaches have been widely implemented or proven effective across all EU member states.

The evidence suggests strong thematic agreement on the importance of coherence, but there is a tension between technical alignment approaches and the argument that incoherence is fundamentally political.

query: What did the interviews with retailers and service providers in North America reveal about managing product returns sustainably?
draft_answer: Interviews with multichannel retailers, retail experts, and return service providers in the UK and North America found that retailers were mainly focused on the financial impact of returns and had little awareness of the scale of environmental impacts, which meant they lacked a comprehensive approach to managing returns sustainably [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||001]. The same study reported barriers that prevent retailers from developing environmental sustainability plans for returns management, and it proposed strategies and a framework for reducing the environmental impact of returns [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||001]. A related interview-based study suggested that sustainability paradoxes can arise in sustainable practices, including handling product returns, and advised retailers to avoid these paradoxes by shifting toward cradle-to-cradle, closed-loop lifecycle supply chains [https://openalex.org/W3135380255||ABSTRACT||001]. That study also recommended that retailers evaluate whether the practices they adopt actually support sustainability and consider the full supply chain and each agent’s role in creating sustained competitive advantage [https://openalex.org/W3135380255||ABSTRACT||001]. Across the evidence, a common theme is that sustainable returns management requires looking beyond immediate financial metrics toward broader lifecycle and supply-chain effects [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3135380255||ABSTRACT||001]. More generally, other papers in the set support the importance of circular approaches, such as product recovery in circular supply chains and reuse-oriented distribution systems, while also noting barriers like lack of collaboration, policy support, expertise, technology, and information [https://openalex.org/W4312219350||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4205116137||ABSTRACT||000].
